title: Occasion and date
short: An elegy for Arthur Henry Hallam (d. Vienna, Sept. 1833), written c. 1834-35 and first printed in Tennyson's Poems (1842).
body: Tennyson's closest Cambridge friend, Arthur Hallam, died suddenly in Vienna on 15 September 1833, aged twenty-two. This lyric belongs to the first wave of grief that also produced the earliest sections of In Memoriam (1850), 'Ulysses' and 'Tithonus'. Tennyson's own note, printed in the Memoir, says it was 'made in a Lincolnshire lane at five o'clock in the morning, between blossoming hedges'; biographers place it in 1834 or early 1835, Martin linking it to a stay at Mablethorpe on the Lincolnshire coast. The archive's heading (1843) refers to the second edition of the 1842 Poems. The poem names no one: its power lies in withholding the dead man's identity, so that the grief is general as well as personal.

title: Metre and the opening spondees
short: Three heavy monosyllables, each a full stress, imitate the slow fall of waves; the rest moves in loose three-beat lines.
body: The poem is in four quatrains rhymed abcb, the pattern of the ballad stanza, but the lines are irregular trimeters mixing anapaests and iambs (for example 'O well for the fisherman's boy'). The first line is exceptional: three stressed syllables separated by pauses, so that each 'break' takes the time of a whole foot and mimics the separate fall of three waves. The command is addressed to the sea, but the word also points to the speaker's breaking heart and to the break in his life. The line returns at l. 13, giving the poem a refrain-like frame; the second time the waves break 'At the foot of thy crags', marking a hardening from stones to cliffs.

title: The inexpressible
short: The speaker wishes he could speak his thoughts: grief is presented as beyond language, a recurrent theme of Tennyson's elegies.
body: 'I would that' is an archaic optative, 'I wish that'. The paradox, familiar in elegy, is that a poem announces its own inability to say what it feels. In Memoriam V develops the same idea ('I sometimes hold it half a sin / To put in words the grief I feel'). Critics have noted that the sea, which ceaselessly 'breaks' and makes sound, contrasts with the speaker's blocked utterance; nature can express itself, the mourner cannot. The poem's own extreme plainness of diction is a form of this reticence.

anchor: O well for the fisherman's boy
title: O well for ...
short: 'O well for' means 'it is well for, happy is': the children and sailor, untouched by loss, live wholly in the present.
body: The construction is an old exclamatory form of congratulation, close to the biblical beatitude ('Blessed are ...'). The fisherman's boy shouting with his sister and the sailor lad singing are images of unselfconscious voice, set against the speaker who cannot 'utter'. They also represent ordinary life continuing indifferently around a private grief, a motif Tennyson returns to in In Memoriam VII, where 'on the bald street breaks the blank day'. The brother-and-sister pair may glance at Hallam's engagement to Tennyson's sister Emily, though this is a biographical inference, not something the poem states.

title: The stately ships
short: Ships passing on to harbour suggest lives completing their courses, and perhaps a peaceful death, while the speaker is left behind.
body: The ships 'go on' to their destination, a phrase that stresses continuation; the world's business proceeds. Their 'haven under the hill' is a sheltered harbour beneath a headland, but the phrase also carries the old association of the haven as the soul's rest after the voyage of life. Some readers hear in 'under the hill' a hint of burial; Hallam was buried in January 1834 in the church at Clevedon, Somerset, on a hill above the Bristol Channel, though there is no evidence Tennyson intended the reference. The contrast is between purposeful motion and the speaker's static lament.

title: haven
short: A harbour; the word recalls Psalm 107, where God brings storm-tossed sailors 'unto their desired haven'.
body: 'Haven' is an old English word for a harbour or port (OED), long used figuratively for a place of rest and safety. The Prayer Book and King James versions of Psalm 107 describe those who 'go down to the sea in ships' and are brought, after the storm, to 'their desired haven' (v. 30); the psalm was familiar from the Prayer Book, including its forms of prayer at sea. The allusion, if felt, deepens the gap: the ships reach their haven, the speaker finds no comfort.

anchor: the touch of a vanish'd hand
title: The vanished hand and the still voice
short: The poem's emotional centre: grief is felt through the senses of touch and hearing, the most physical traces of a lost friend.
body: 'O for' expresses longing ('would that I had'). Touch and voice are the two signs of Hallam's bodily presence that Tennyson repeatedly mourns: in In Memoriam VII he waits at Hallam's door in Wimpole Street 'A hand that can be clasp'd no more'. 'Vanish'd' (the archive keeps Tennyson's elided spelling) suggests disappearance rather than death, a sudden removal. A voice 'that is still' means silent; it may also hint at 'still' in the sense of 'continuing', a double meaning some readers find in Tennyson's usage, though most editors take it simply as 'silenced'. The line is among the best-known expressions of Victorian bereavement.

anchor: At the foot of thy crags
title: crags
short: Steep rocks or cliffs; the shift from 'stones' to 'crags' in the repeated stanza makes the barrier more forbidding.
body: The Lincolnshire coast near Mablethorpe, where the poem has been associated, is flat and sandy, so the 'crags' are not a literal description; editors treat the seascape as composite or imagined. Within the poem, the change from the 'cold gray stones' of l. 2 to 'crags' raises the scale of the obstacle: the sea breaks against something it cannot alter, as the speaker's grief beats against the fact of death. The return of the opening line with a variation is a typical device of song.

anchor: the tender grace of a day
title: The tender grace of a day that is dead
short: The poem ends not with consolation but with the irrecoverable past; 'grace' means charm and gentle favour, perhaps also blessing.
body: 'Grace' here means beauty of a delicate kind and the favour of a happier time; the religious sense of divine grace may hover, given the absence of any explicit Christian comfort. The personification of a 'day that is dead' transfers death from the friend to time itself. The closing line, 'Will never come back to me', refuses the movement from grief to hope that In Memoriam would later make. The poem shares this sense of the lost past with 'Tears, idle tears', whose refrain is 'the days that are no more'.
